title: Build a new hire onboarding assistant
description: A system that walks new hires through their first-week checklist day by day and tracks what's done.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

slack.title: Slack
slack.content: The team messaging app most companies run on. In Level 2, students connect Slack to their AI tools to trigger workflows from messages, post AI-generated updates to channels, or summarize threads automatically.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

notion.title: Notion
notion.content: An all-in-one workspace for docs, wikis, databases, and project tracking. Used heavily across the AI Builder program as a destination for AI-generated content and as a connected app in Level 2 automations.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

children.text: Only 12% of employees strongly agree their company does a great job onboarding new hires, per [Gallup's research on onboarding and retention](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/235121/why-onboarding-experience-key-retention.aspx). Turnover in the first 18 months can run as high as 50%, and replacing someone can cost six to nine months of salary, per the same report. This system runs a first-week checklist itself, one day at a time, for every new hire.

It sends that day's tasks only, confirms a task done when the new hire says so, and answers setup questions from your IT and HR documentation. Anything outside that documentation escalates to a named contact. At week's end it sends the manager or HR contact a completion summary naming anything still open.

Run it as a paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) you kick off each Monday, a saved [skill](#tooltip-skill), or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that messages the new hire directly. None of it replaces the person who should still be checking in.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming your checklist source, who owns each item, the delivery channel, and what should always escalate to a person.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that walks new hires through their first week and tracks what's done. Ask me questions, one at a time, about what a first-week checklist actually includes today, who owns making sure each item gets done, what new hires ask about most in week one, and where this checklist currently lives. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview forces you to name who owns each checklist item today, which is usually the part nobody has written down.

items: Where the first-week checklist currently lives and who last updated it.
Whether new hires get this through [Slack](#tooltip-slack), email, or a portal.
Whether IT and access provisioning is already automated or still a manual request.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it in a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) first. Then gather any access it calls for. That's your HRIS (Workday, Rippling, Gusto), your messaging platform for delivery, and your IT provisioning system if requests route through one. The paste-in version needs none.
**Create.** Build and test the system on a real new hire's first week. The prompt below is one example; your scope document has the full version.

children.prompt:
Goal: Walk [new hire name] through their day-by-day first-week checklist for the [role/department] track and report completion status to [manager/HR contact].

Context: Checklist source: [doc/link]. Start date: [date]. Tools/access the new hire needs set up: [list].

Rules:
- Send one day's tasks at a time, not the whole week at once.
- Confirm each task as complete only when the new hire says so, never assume.
- Answer setup questions using the provided IT/HR documentation only, and escalate anything outside it to [contact].
- Send a completion summary to [manager/HR contact] at the end of week one flagging anything still open.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: one day's tasks at a time keeps week one from landing as a wall of homework, and confirming by the new hire's word instead of a deadline matches how first weeks go.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. One day at a time, escalations routed correctly, summary sent at week's end?
**Feedback.** Tell it exactly what went wrong ("day 3 tasks arrived before day 2 was done") and fold each correction into the rules.

items: Extend it past week one into a 30/60/90-day check-in cadence.
Auto-flag a new hire falling behind on checklist items for manager follow-up.
Feed completion data back into a broader onboarding-effectiveness report.
Pair it with an HR help desk build so new hires get consistent answers from day one.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric). Have your AI chat turn the scope bar into pass/fail checks and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each new hire's first week, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for new hire, start date, tasks assigned, tasks confirmed complete, and escalations raised. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the guesswork, and the log columns surface a stalling checklist item after a few new hires instead of one at a time.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Note the date, which checks passed or failed, and what changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the rubric passes a few new hires straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill, so every run starts from your defaults. A repeated failure earns its own skill. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write it, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).
One durable failure mode. Tracking task completion isn't the same as a good onboarding experience. Build in at least one moment where a real person checks in.

items: [Gallup, Why the Onboarding Experience Is Key for Retention](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/235121/why-onboarding-experience-key-retention.aspx) — The 12% onboarding-satisfaction figure.
SHRM data, cited in Gallup's onboarding retention research — The 50% first-18-month turnover and six-to-nine-month replacement cost figures.
